name: Ghanaian Waakye
description: Waakye, rice and beans cooked together until they take on a real reddish-brown color, depends on that color to genuinely be waakye - without it, it's just rice and beans, as Ghanaian cooks are fond of saying. Real preparation uses dried millet or sorghum leaves; baking soda is the honest, widely-used traditional substitute when those leaves aren't available, working through the same alkaline reaction to shift the color and help soften the beans.

steps_detailed: Cook the cowpeas with the baking soda and a splash of water 10-12 minutes.
Add the rice and enough water to cook it through, 18-20 minutes, until the rice and beans are tender and take on a real reddish-brown tint from the baking soda's reaction.

name: Ghanaian Jollof Rice
description: Jollof rice, tomato-and-pepper rice cooked until it takes on real color and depth, is fiercely championed in Ghana as the true original in West Africa's long-running jollof rivalry - the real base is a fried, reduced tomato-pepper puree, not just rice simmered in canned sauce.

steps_detailed: Blend the tomatoes, bell pepper, jalapeño, and half the onion into a smooth puree.
Brown the chicken, 6-7 minutes, then set aside.
Fry the remaining onion, add the tomato paste, cook 2 minutes, then add the puree and simmer uncovered 15-18 minutes until deeply reduced.
Stir in the rice, broth, and chicken, cover, and cook on low 20-25 minutes until tender.

name: Ghanaian Banku
description: Banku, fermented corn and cassava dough cooked into a smooth, stretchy paste, is a genuine Ghanaian staple, traditionally eaten by hand alongside soup or grilled fish.
steps_detailed: Mix the cornmeal and grated cassava with water into a smooth batter and let sit at room temperature 12-24 hours to ferment - real banku's sour tang comes from this fermentation, not an ingredient added directly.
Cook the fermented batter over medium heat, stirring constantly, 15-18 minutes, until thick, smooth, and stretchy.

name: Ghanaian Kenkey
description: Kenkey, fermented corn dough wrapped in corn husks or banana leaves and steamed, is a genuine Ghanaian staple with a distinctive sour tang from real fermentation, real technique dividing the fermented dough into portions and cooking part of it first into a thick porridge before combining, which gives kenkey its characteristic dense, slightly gummy texture.
steps_detailed: Mix the cornmeal with water into a stiff dough and let ferment at room temperature 24 hours.
Cook about a third of the fermented dough with a little water into a thick paste, then knead it back into the remaining raw dough along with the salt.
Shape into balls, wrap tightly, and steam over simmering water 45-50 minutes until firm and cooked through.

name: Ghanaian Groundnut Soup
description: Groundnut soup, built on real ground peanuts, is one of Ghana's most beloved soups, traditionally served with fufu or rice, real versions finished with a real pinch of chili for background heat.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

ingredients.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

steps_detailed: Brown the chicken with the onion, 6-7 minutes.
Whisk the ground peanuts with 1.5 cups water into a smooth paste.
Add the peanut paste, tomatoes, and jalapeño, and simmer 20-25 minutes until thickened and the chicken is tender.

name: Ghanaian Kelewele
description: Kelewele, spiced fried ripe plantain, is a beloved Ghanaian street food, real ground ginger being the defining flavor, traditionally cut into irregular chunks rather than neat slices.
steps_detailed: Toss the plantain with the fresh ginger and chili powder.
Fry, turning, 4-5 minutes, until deeply caramelized.

name: Ghanaian Red Red
description: Red red, black-eyed peas stewed in palm-oil-red tomato sauce and served with fried plantain, gets its name from the color of both the beans' sauce and the plantain.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Simmer the cowpeas with the tomatoes and palm oil 12-15 minutes.
Fry the plantain slices in a separate pan, 3-4 minutes per side, until caramelized.
Serve the beans with the fried plantain alongside.

name: Ghanaian Fufu
description: Fufu, cassava and plantain pounded together into a smooth, stretchy dough, is one of West Africa's most iconic staple starches, traditionally eaten by tearing off pieces to scoop up soup, real technique boiling both starches until genuinely soft before pounding, since underdone starch won't pound smooth.
steps_detailed: Boil the cassava and plantain together until completely soft, 20-25 minutes - a fork should go in with no resistance.
Drain well and pound vigorously and continuously until smooth and stretchy, free of lumps.
steps: Boil the cassava and plantain together until completely soft, 20-25 minutes - a fork should go in with no resistance.

name: Ghanaian Light Soup
description: Light soup, a thin, peppery tomato broth, is a common Ghanaian everyday soup, lighter than groundnut or palm nut soup, real technique letting the tomatoes cook down fully so the broth builds real depth rather than tasting watery.
steps_detailed: Combine the chicken, tomatoes, jalapeño, onion, and garlic in 2 cups water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook 25-30 minutes, uncovered, so the broth reduces slightly and the tomatoes fully break down, until the chicken is tender.

name: Ghanaian Shito
description: Shito, a fiery, dark pepper and dried fish sauce, is one of Ghana's most essential condiments, spooned onto nearly anything, real depth coming from a real, patient fry.
steps_detailed: Blend the jalapeño and onion into a coarse paste.
Fry the paste in the oil over medium heat, stirring often, 15-18 minutes, until deeply dark and reduced - this long fry is what gives real shito its depth.
Stir in the fish sauce off the heat.

description: Chichinga, spiced grilled meat skewers coated in a ground peanut rub, closely related to Nigerian suya and shared across the wider West African region.

ingredients.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

steps_detailed: Mix the ground peanuts with the paprika and chili powder.
Coat the sliced beef in the mixture and thread onto skewers.
Grill, turning, 6-8 minutes, until charred.

name: Ghanaian Tatale
description: Tatale, sweet, spiced ripe plantain pancakes, is a beloved Ghanaian breakfast, real technique using genuinely overripe, heavily spotted plantain, since its natural sugars are what make tatale sweet without needing added sugar.
steps_detailed: Mix the mashed plantain with the flour and ginger into a thick batter - it should hold its shape on a spoon.
Fry spoonfuls, flattening slightly, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply golden and cooked through in the center.
